goal.title: The goal
paragraphs: Grow your net worth: the cash you hold, plus what your companies own, less what they owe. There is no end; play as long as you like.
You start with one business and some money. Run it well, open or buy more, and keep clear of unpaid bills.

time.title: Time
paragraphs: The clock at the bottom runs a day at a time, at the speed you pick, or a week at once. What you change applies at the start of the next day, and waits in the list above the clock until then.
The clock stops for news you choose (menu, When to pause), and the game saves itself every month and when you leave.

holding.title: Your holding
paragraphs: The dashboard shows your net worth, what needs doing, each store at a glance, your profit week by week, and the news.

Each company has its finances: put your money into it, pay yourself a dividend out of its profit (the state takes 30%), and borrow. The bank lends on what your stores earn, and more if you guarantee it yourself; open or buy a store without the cash and it offers to lend the rest.

store.title: Your store
paragraphs: Choose what is on the shelves and at what price, against what shoppers in that city think normal. Staff each part of the day: too few and shoppers wait or walk out; none and the store is shut.
Spend a share of sales on marketing to build goodwill, hire a manager to run things for you, enlarge the store, or turn a convenience store into a supermarket.

Holding lists your companies. Hire a director for any of them there: they hire the managers, close stores that keep losing money, grow it as far as you allow, borrowing if you let them, and write to you each month.
Start a subsidiary from Holding to keep a new business apart: it has its own cash, books, loans and director, and if it fails the rest is safe.

orders.title: Orders
paragraphs: Buy stock from suppliers. Each has its lead time, payment terms, minimum order and discounts. Fresh food spoils, so order what will sell before it does.

reports.title: Reports
paragraphs: See profit and loss week by week or month by month, where shoppers came from and went, and what they wanted and could not find. Buy market studies to learn about a city before you open there.

market.title: The market
paragraphs: Follow the economy: inflation, the central bank's rate and unemployment rise and fall through booms and recessions, and shoppers spend accordingly. Profit is taxed every January.
Companies publish their accounts each year. See every rival, its stores and prices, and the cities with their vacant sites.

deals.title: Buying and selling businesses
paragraphs: Every store has an asking price: its fittings and stock, plus a few years of what it earns beyond a fair return on them. A store losing money sells for well under what it holds, a bargain for whoever can turn it round.

Buy a rival's store with one of your companies' cash, borrowing the rest on what both earn, or a whole company with its stores, cash and debts out of your own pocket, the company borrowing part of its price on its own earnings. Sell a store to the chain best able to pay. Gains are taxed with the year's profit; rivals buy struggling stores too.

tips.title: Tips
paragraphs: Keep the shelves stocked: shoppers who find them empty go elsewhere, and some stay there.

Price close to what shoppers expect; dear works where people can afford it. Cutting prices wins shoppers, but most leave when prices rise, and thin margins earn little in a small shop: discounting pays on a supermarket's volume, or for a few months to start a new store.

Watch the cash. A bill unpaid for a month means liquidation, and a recession can empty the till. Each company keeps a cushion for wages, rent, loan payments and January's tax: below it, managers buy only the essentials.
